Then she put it back in its bag, not carefully, and started the engine again. The tick had gone. That was the kind of thing he would have laughed at, a fault that cured itself the moment you stopped needing it not to.

She did not turn for home. She had told herself she would, at six hours, and she had meant it, but the boat kept its heading as if it had opinions of its own. The haze thickened ahead. Somewhere in it there was a coast she had never seen, or nothing at all, and she found she could hold both possibilities at once without much trouble. He had said that was the trick. Not hoping. Just keeping the two doors open and walking down the corridor between them.

The second apple she ate finally, core and all, because throwing anything over the side felt like an announcement. The taste was sharp and ordinary and made her want to cry, so she concentrated on the compass instead, on the way the needle shivered and settled, shivered and settled.
